This felt like watching an episode of Blue Bloods. Honestly I really didn’t like this movie. Maybe that’s sacrilege because it’s Scorsese but it just felt pointless. Many of Scorsese’s movies fall somewhere between “not my cup of tea but I can tell it’s well made” and “this is the greatest movie ever.” But this one doesn’t even reach the former. In terms of artisanship it felt really all over the place. The camera does weirdly intense tracking shots for something as simple as pulling out a cell phone, but for 90% of the important character motions it’s just simple medium shots and shot-reverse-shot conversations. It felt like that scene in SpongeBob where he makes the first word of his essay super ornamental but forgets to spend any time on the rest. In general I just don’t love the subject matter of most Scorsese movies. The whole film consists of hotheaded cops punching each other out and gangsters swinging their dicks to see who can sound the toughest. It’s so tired. I can never tell whether Scorsese is trying to make a jaded, gritty movie about the blurred lines between good and bad men, or whether he’s trying to make a movie about the good old days when you could punch a cop, kiss a dame, and Coca Cola cost a nickel. It also feels like there’s a lot of “symbolism” or “poignant” stuff in this movie that I just don’t connect with. Like wow it ends with a rat crawling on the balcony. Get it? Cause the movies about “rats”? The movie rolls credits with “The Departed” in like the second scene by talking about the victims of Costello’s crimes, then proceeds to not be about that idea in any way for the rest of the movie. What is this movie trying to say? On top of all of that it’s honestly just a gross movie. You can’t make it 3 lines without some form of expletive, slur, or innuendo. I’m sure that’s supposed to be its “style” and maybe that’s just how Boston is, but I really don’t need to hear for the 4th time in as many scenes how much Jack Nicholson fucks. Bad movie and I dont really get what people see in it.

Where the original finds tragedy in the erosion of identity, The Departed seems more interested in watching a room full of men compete to see who can swear the loudest. Infernal Affairs is about two men losing themselves. The Departed is about Hollywood losing its indoor voice.

Is this Scorsese’s best? No. I’d give that to Goodfellas. It’s still wildly entertaining though. We get a great cat and mouse game between DiCaprio and Damon where Scorsese is great at ratcheting up the tension, with the silent phone call scene being a great example. It helps that we care about both characters. While it would be simple to root for the undercover cop which I do, part of me wants the undercover crim to get away with it. Throw in a great supporting cast on top of their game from Mark Wahlberg (he’s a nice guy if you get to know him), Martin Sheen, Vera Farmiga, Ray Winstone and Alec Baldwin who really looks like he’s enjoying his role. Then of course there’s Jack, in what might be one of his last memorable performances, who brings an energy where I wouldn’t want to work for him but I wouldn’t be opposed to having a beer with him. Interestingly being a loyal LA guy he refused to wear a Boston cap. To top it off we get a great soundtrack including Scorsese favorite Gimme Shelter, I’m Shipping off to Boston and Comfortably Numb. The ending, without giving away spoilers, may turn some people off. The person sitting behind me was audibly shocked, however the more I’ve seen it the more I like it.
